script_blocks: Fifty thousand dollars. That is what one of these houses cost about ten years ago, on these exact streets, in this exact zip code. A real estate agent who works the neighborhood put it plainly: a vacant lot or a boarded house here may have gone for fifty or sixty thousand a decade back, and today the same dirt asks two hundred fifty thousand, if not more. Nobody moved the ocean. Nobody discovered oil under Liberty City. The house did not get bigger. In a lot of cases the house did not even get renovated, not really. It got paint, it got floors, it got a new air conditioner, and it got a new number on the listing. I want to tell you about one woman who looked at that arithmetic and did something almost nobody in her position does. She did not complain about it. She did not write a letter to the county. She started buying. Her name is Ernisha Randolph, and she is part of something called the Miami Millennial Investment Group. When a television reporter asked her why young Black investors were putting their own money into Overtown, Liberty City and Opa-locka, she gave an answer so blunt it has stuck with me ever since. Instead of complaining about it, she said, because that is not going to change much, we might as well get in the game. Get in the game. Think about what that sentence is actually admitting. It admits the game exists, that it has rules, that the rules are not fair, and that standing outside the stadium shouting at it has not worked. By the time that interview aired, her group had already bought thirteen houses. Now here is the part I could not get out of my head, and the reason this is not a simple story about a clever investor. There is a man a few streets over named Broadway Cuthbert Harewood. He bought his first property in nineteen eighty-seven. He has lived through every boom and every bust this city has had. And he told a reporter that he gets a minimum of thirty calls a day from investors who want his house. Thirty. Every single day. He hangs up on all of them. So the question that runs underneath this entire episode is this. Why do the homeowners of Liberty City slam the phone down on thirty investors a day, and then hand their keys to this one?

Let me back up and describe the ground we are standing on, because if you have never been to Miami you are probably picturing the wrong thing entirely. When people say Miami they picture Miami Beach. Glass towers, water on both sides, a Lamborghini double-parked outside a restaurant where a salad costs more than a tank of gas. Liberty City is not that. Liberty City is inland, a few miles northwest of downtown, low houses on a flat grid, concrete block construction, chain link, mango trees older than the mortgages. It is one of the historically Black neighborhoods of Miami, and for most of the last fifty years the money that flooded into this city flowed around it the way water flows around a stone. And then something happened that nobody planned and nobody can reverse. Liberty City sits ten to fifteen feet above sea level. On one map it is twelve. If you have spent any time thinking about South Florida you already know why that number matters. Miami Beach is essentially at sea level. Much of the glamorous coastline is three, four, five feet up. Twelve feet, in a city where the sea is measurably rising, is not just a number on a survey. It is the highest ground for miles. For a century, that elevation was worth nothing, because nobody wanted to be far from the water. The whole point of Miami was the water. Then the water started coming up the storm drains on sunny days, and insurance got expensive, and suddenly being twelve feet up and five miles inland stopped looking like a consolation prize. Researchers have a name for what follows. They call it climate gentrification, and Liberty City is the case study everybody cites. I want to be careful here, because this is the part where a lot of coverage gets sloppy. Elevation is not the only thing driving prices in this neighborhood, and anybody who tells you it is has an agenda. There is also a two hundred and twenty million dollar public and private redevelopment of Liberty Square, the public housing complex at the heart of the neighborhood. There is the ordinary spillover from Wynwood and Little Haiti, where the art galleries and the breweries arrived first. There is the simple fact that Miami ran out of cheap land. Elevation is one line in the ledger. It is a real line. It is not the whole page. But whatever the cause, the effect is brutally easy to measure, and this is where the numbers start to get uncomfortable. A couple named Naomie and Errick Pigatt bought their house about thirteen years ago for roughly one hundred thirty thousand dollars. It is now estimated to be worth about five hundred eighty thousand. A man named Steven Carroll bought in two thousand five for about one hundred thirty-five thousand. His house is now worth somewhere around four hundred thousand. As of this spring, the median asking price in one Liberty City zip code, thirty-three thousand one twenty-seven, had pushed above six hundred sixty thousand dollars. A new four-bedroom on the market there was listed at nine hundred twenty-five thousand. Nine hundred twenty-five thousand dollars. In the neighborhood that the rest of Miami spent fifty years driving past.

So let us talk about the actual mechanics, because this is the part that nobody explains properly and it is the part that makes the whole thing work. When people hear house flipping they picture a television show. Sledgehammer through a wall, a designer in a hard hat, a granite island the size of a small boat. That is the expensive version, and in a neighborhood like this it is usually the wrong version. The money in Miami is not in the gut renovation. The money is in what the trade politely calls cosmetic work. A cosmetic flip is exactly what it sounds like. You do not move a wall. You do not touch the roof structure. You do not rewire the house. You paint every surface white, because white photographs larger. You tear out whatever is on the floor and put down one continuous cheap hard surface, because a single uninterrupted floor also photographs larger. You replace the kitchen cabinet fronts, or if the budget is thin you paint them and change the handles. You put in a new air conditioner, which in South Florida is not cosmetic at all, it is the single appliance a buyer will actually test. You clean the yard down to the dirt and lay sod. You pressure wash the driveway. And then you photograph it with a wide lens on an overcast morning and you list it. Notice what is absent from that list. Nothing structural. Nothing that requires the slow, expensive, publicly recorded permits that a real renovation requires. That absence is the business model. Every week a house sits waiting on an inspector is a week of interest on the loan that bought it. Here is a documented example of what that spread looks like in this neighborhood, and I want to be precise that this is a company, not our protagonist. An outfit called Crusader Capital Group bought homes in the area for between three hundred thousand and three hundred sixty thousand dollars, and flipped them for between five hundred sixty thousand and six hundred thousand. Run the middle of that. Buy at three hundred thirty, sell at five hundred eighty. Two hundred fifty thousand dollars of gross spread on one house. Take out the paint, the floors, the air conditioner, the sod, the closing costs, the loan interest, the realtor commission, the property taxes for the months you held it. Say all of it comes to eighty thousand, and I am being generous, because a cosmetic job on a small concrete block house in Florida can be done for a fraction of that. You are still walking away with something in the neighborhood of a hundred and seventy thousand dollars. For paint, floors, and an air conditioner. And now you understand the thirty phone calls a day. Those are not random calls. That is a spread of a hundred and seventy thousand dollars per house, sitting on a street where the people who own the houses are mostly older, mostly on fixed incomes, and mostly have no idea what the house two doors down just closed for. Every one of those thirty calls is somebody doing that math in their head before they dial.

Which brings me to the ugliest number in this entire story, and the one I think about most. Steven Carroll, the man who bought in two thousand five for a hundred thirty-five thousand, had just finished renovating his own home. His own money, his own work, his own house that he has lived in for more than twenty years. He is not some abstract figure either. He is the son of Earl J. Carroll, the first Black Miami-Dade commissioner. His family has been part of the civic architecture of this county for generations. A caller offered him just over two hundred thousand dollars. For a house currently valued around four hundred thousand. Freshly renovated. Half. Roughly half of what it is worth, offered to the son of the first Black county commissioner, on the assumption that he would not know the difference. I have spent a long time in stories about people getting a fraction of what their property is worth. Usually it is a painting in an attic, a coin in a jar, a guitar at a yard sale, and usually the person who got underpaid genuinely did not know. That is the whole shape of the genre. Somebody did not know, somebody else did, and the gap between them is where the money went. This is not that. This is the same shape, but the object is a house, and the person who did not know is supposed to be the one who lives in it. That is the difference between a lucky antique dealer and something that deserves a harder word. And the mechanism scales. A real estate agent in the neighborhood, Bernard Phanord, who also runs an organization called the Collective Empowerment Group, is the one who gave that fifty-to-two-hundred-fifty thousand comparison. He watches it happen. Robert Jones, the communications director of something called the SMILE Trust, works the same ground. Elaine Black runs the Liberty City Community Revitalization Trust. These are not activists shouting from outside. These are people who understand the paperwork as well as any investor does, and who have watched the paperwork be used as a weapon. So what do you do? You cannot outlaw a phone call. You cannot make it illegal to offer somebody money for their house. You cannot legislate a neighborhood into staying cheap, and frankly you should not want to, because the people who own those houses are the ones whose net worth just quadrupled. The Pigatts went from a hundred thirty thousand to five hundred eighty thousand. That is real. That is generational money, if they can hold on to it. The problem was never that the houses got valuable. The problem is who gets to be standing there when they do.

And that is the answer to the question I opened with. That is why the keys go to one investor and not the other thirty. Because the thirty calls a day all end the same way. Somebody outside the neighborhood buys the house cheap, paints it white, sells it high, and takes the spread somewhere else. The money passes through the street without stopping. The house stays. The paint stays. The family does not. What Ernisha Randolph and the Miami Millennial Investment Group did was change exactly one variable in that equation, and it is not the one you would guess. They did not pay more. They did not renovate more honestly. They changed who the buyer of last resort is, and where the person who ends up living in the house comes from. There is a woman named Valencia Gunder, a Liberty City activist, and here is the detail that made this whole story click for me. She was renting from the Miami Millennial Investment Group, with the stated goal of buying the house she was living in. Read that again, because it is the entire argument in one sentence. The investor bought the cheap house. The investor fixed the cheap house. And then the investor rented it to somebody from the neighborhood on a path to owning it. That is the same transaction as the flip. Buy low, improve, transfer at a higher value. Identical arithmetic. Completely different outcome, because the higher value lands on a resident instead of leaving in a car. I am not going to stand here and tell you this is a solution. Thirteen houses is thirteen houses. Liberty City has thousands. Against a two hundred and twenty million dollar redevelopment and an entire market of investors dialing thirty times a day into every phone on the block, thirteen houses is a rounding error, and anybody selling you thirteen houses as the answer to climate gentrification is selling you something. But I do think it is the most interesting thirteen houses in Miami. Because they prove a thing that is very easy to forget when you watch a market do something ugly. The ugliness was never in the arithmetic. Buy cheap, fix, sell higher is not a moral position, it is just subtraction. Two people can run the identical subtraction and one of them hollows out a neighborhood and the other one hands somebody a deed. Same math. Opposite result. The variable is who is holding the pencil.

So where does it stand now, and what actually happens next. The pressure has not stopped, it has intensified. The vacant properties that went for fifty or sixty thousand a decade ago are asking two hundred fifty and up. Zillow puts the neighborhood average somewhere around four hundred thirty thousand. That one zip code is above six hundred sixty thousand at the median. New construction is testing nine hundred twenty-five thousand. The Liberty Square redevelopment is two hundred twenty million dollars of committed money, and money that size does not arrive quietly. Broadway Cuthbert Harewood is still getting his thirty calls a day. He bought his first property in nineteen eighty-seven, which means he has now owned through the savings and loan mess, through Hurricane Andrew, through the two thousand eight collapse when Miami-Dade was one of the worst foreclosure markets in the country, and through whatever we are calling this. He is not selling. Some of his neighbors will. If you take one practical thing from this episode, let it be this, and it applies whether you own a house in Liberty City or a chest of drawers in your grandmother's garage. The person who calls you already knows the number. That is the entire reason they are calling. Nobody spends money on a list of phone numbers to offer strangers a fair price. The offer you get unsolicited is, by construction, the offer that is good for the person making it. Steven Carroll was offered two hundred thousand for a four hundred thousand dollar house, and the only thing standing between him and that loss was that he happened to know what he had. Find out what you have. Not from the buyer. Ever. That is also the most honest lesson from Ernisha Randolph, and it has nothing to do with real estate. She did not get a better outcome by being angrier than everybody else, or more informed in some abstract way. She got a better outcome by getting on the same side of the table as the people with the spreadsheets. Instead of complaining about it, because that is not going to change much, we might as well get in the game. Thirteen houses. So far. If this one held you, the full arithmetic of how a fifty thousand dollar house becomes a six hundred thousand dollar listing is the kind of thing this channel takes apart for a living, and there is a lot more of it. Stay for the next one.

youtube.description_intro:
Ten years ago a boarded-up house in Liberty City went for fifty or sixty thousand dollars. Today the same dirt asks two hundred fifty thousand and up, and one zip code in the neighborhood has a median above six hundred sixty thousand. Nobody moved the ocean. In most cases nobody even really renovated the house — it got paint, floors, an air conditioner and a new number on the listing.

This is the story of the arithmetic behind that, and of Ernisha Randolph, who looked at it and decided the only move left was to get in the game. It is also the story of a man who gets thirty investor calls a day and hangs up on every one, and of a homeowner who was offered roughly half of what his freshly renovated house was worth.

Same subtraction, opposite result. The variable is who is holding the pencil.
youtube.description_notes: A note on what is verified and what is not. The Liberty City price figures, the thirty calls a day, the lowball offer and the Crusader Capital buy-and-flip range are reported by WLRN and The Miami Times (May 2026). Ernisha Randolph's quote and the thirteen homes bought by the Miami Millennial Investment Group are from NBC 6 South Florida (September 2018); no purchase or sale prices for that group have been published, and none are claimed here. The Crusader Capital numbers belong to that company and not to Randolph — they are used only to show what the spread looks like in this neighborhood. Climate gentrification is one documented driver of prices here, not the only one.
